newsitem.title: IRAN: Iran's Khatami could clash with conservatives.
newsitem.headline: Iran's Khatami could clash with conservatives.

text.p: New President Mohammad Khatami, sworn in on Monday, could enjoy a "honeymoon" with Iran's Western critics, but on the home front analysts predicted a tough struggle to get his cabinet list approved by the conservative parliament.
Moderate Khatami has so far kept his cabinet list under wraps, but must present it to parliament for approval within two weeks.
"The first few weeks will be like a honeymoon period, waiting to see if there are signs of change before deciding on the next move," said a Gulf-based Western diplomat.

Khatami, 54, has yet to announce his cabinet list but it is expected to include representatives of various groups which gave him an overwhelming election victory and at the same time seek to appease religious hardliners.
After taking the oath of office, Khatami said Iran would not take any actions which could create world tension.
"My government considers dialogue between civilisations in the present world essential and will avoid any action or behaviour causing tension," he told parliament.
"He has put a positive spin on his message," one Western diplomat in Tehran said. "We now have to see how far this will carry anyone."

Iran's United Nations' envoy Kamal Kharrazi could be the man who takes on the difficult mission of improving the image of Tehran - accused by several regional and world powers of supporting international "terrorism". Iran denies the charge.

Kharrazi told Reuters on Monday he had been approached to head the foreign ministry -- replacing U.S.-educated Ali Akbar Velayati who has held the post since two years after the 1979 Islamic revolution.
"There have been disussions with me," he said. When asked if he had accepted, Kharrazi said: "But we have to wait until the cabinet is presented to parliament."

Diplomats in Tehran said Khatami would probably concentrate on domestic issues in the early days of his presidency, using the overwhelming majority which elected him to consolidate his power in face of influential conservative forces.
Supreme leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei said on Sunday his confirmation of Khatami as well as the vote of the people remained "valid" as long as long he followed the divine teachings of Islam.

Parliament speaker, Ali Akbar Nateq-Nouri, and the head of the judiciary, Ayatollah Mohammad Yazdi, both indirectly hinted in speeches at the swearing-in ceremony that Khatami should consult parliament ahead of presenting a cabinet list.
According to the constitution, Khatami has to present his cabinet to parliament within two weeks of taking office.
Khatami re-appointed the uncontroversial Hassan Habibi as first vice-president, a post he already held under outgoing president Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani.
Hours after Khatami sent signs of moderation to the 20 million people who voted for him, Iranians artists toured Tehran cinemas with flowers and sweets to celebrate.
In his address, Khatami repeatedly stressed that the rule of law would prevail in Iran and promised social justice.

"Although it was carefully worded, the message was very strong," an Arab ambassador said after the speech. "He says we (clergymen) must have a dialogue with the people who are the reference point and respect personal freedoms."

Khatami said his main goals were "protecting freedom and respect for the rights of people, expansion and deepening of a civil society, preventing violation of legal rights and liberties and provide freedom of expression and comfort of mind for every individual..."
He was invited to the podium by Nateq-Nouri -- the man originally tipped to win May's presidential elections but who only secured about seven million out of 29.1 million votes.

In another sign of moderation, Khatami told Iran's Moslem Shi'ite theologians not to consider their own interpretations of the Moslem holy book, the Koran, "as the absolute word of God" and called for the free exchange of other views which should be taken into consideration.
